SpecPilot: Autonomous Algorithm Discovery and Systems Optimization for Speculative Decoding

Kunjun Li    Wenhao Chai    Yihao Liang    Yuezhou Hu    Shuyao Xu    Yi Pan    William X. Zheng    Kannan Ramchandran    Kurt Keutzer    Jiantao Jiao Affiliation: [ Affiliation: [ Affiliation: [ Affiliation: [
Abstract

Abstract

Speculative decoding accelerates memory-bound LLM decoding with a lightweight drafter, and parallel drafters extend this speedup by drafting a whole block in one forward pass. However, it remains unclear whether their released systems (stock) attain the full speedup that parallel drafting permits. We identify three challenges. First, with one request, each step accepts few tokens but reads every target weight. Second, with batching, per-request verification work roughly halves the speedup over autoregressive (AR) decoding. Third, speculative decoding is deployment-specific, and no universal optimization fits every serving regime, drafter, target model and GPU. To address these challenges, we present SpecPilot, an autonomous agentic loop that discovers algorithms and systems optimizations for each deployment. In each round, a cost model locates the largest gaps between the current system and its ceiling. Parallel agents explore directions and integrate the successful ones. Token forcing checks every output token against stock to detect reward hacking. A structured memory carries validated mechanisms to new rounds and deployments. SpecPilot discovered a general lossless 12-bit weight format, tree verification for hybrid recurrent targets, two-level verification and three batching mechanisms. We evaluate it across four target models, three drafters, two GPU platforms and five benchmarks. Without training or quality loss, it raises the speedup over AR from stock’s 4.46×\times to 10.87×\times with one request, and from 1.94×\times to 3.93×\times with batching.

1 Introduction

Speculative decoding [1, 2] accelerates memory-bound autoregressive (AR) decoding of large language models (LLMs) with a lightweight drafter, so one target pass accepts several tokens. AR drafters such as EAGLE-3 [3] draft sequentially, while parallel drafters such as DFlash [4], DFlash2 [5] and DSpark [6] draft a block of 8 or 16 tokens per forward pass.

However, their released systems (stock) leave much of this potential unrealized. With one request, reading the target weights dominates the per-step latency (Figure 2a), so verifying additional tokens adds little extra latency. Stock still verifies only one drafted chain, ignoring the other candidates that its drafter ranks at each position, which often include the target’s next token. Using them would accept about twice as many tokens per step (§3.1). With batching, each request adds its own attention, recurrent-state and prefill work, so weight reads no longer dominate the step, and stock’s speedup over AR decoding roughly halves (Figure 2b).

Existing techniques such as draft trees [7, 8, 9, 10] and batch-aware speculation [11, 12, 13] are general, but the best choice depends on the deployment. A deployment comprises a serving regime, a drafter, a target and a GPU platform, and each changes what pays off. The serving regime can turn a gain into a loss. Checking drafts with a low-precision target copy before the exact pass speeds up decoding with one request, but with batching on BF16 Qwen3.8-27B the same idea is 13% slower, because the extra check takes nearly a step. The drafter decides how to score a draft tree. DSpark conditions each drafted token on the one before it, and a tree that ignores this accepts half the tokens of one using it. The target and the GPU decide what each mechanism costs. A tree on hybrid Qwen3.8-27B [14] must track every node’s recurrent state (§2.3), and the RTX PRO 6000 lacks Hopper’s wgmma instructions, so kernels need porting. No universal optimization fits every deployment.

Manually optimizing each deployment does not scale, whereas coding agents [15, 16] iterate rapidly. This makes per-deployment optimization a natural fit for them, and agentic optimizers such as AlphaEvolve and ADRS already evolve programs against automated evaluators [17, 18]. For lossless speculative decoding, however, building a reliable evaluator is difficult for two reasons. First, many gains are only a few percent, close to timing noise, and a gain measured on development requests may not generalize to unseen ones. Second, an agent rewarded for speed is prone to reward hacking [19, 20], such as adopting a faster numerical shortcut that changes outputs without a measurable drop in task accuracy (Figure 2c).

We present SpecPilot (Figure 3), an autonomous agentic loop that searches for speculative decoding optimizations tailored to each deployment. It rests on four ideas. First, a cost model compares measured performance with an estimated ceiling to locate where speed is lost. Second, parallel agents explore multiple directions on separate GPUs and integrate the validated pieces, so small gains add up. Third, a controller isolated from the agents accepts a change only on a significant gain confirmed on unseen requests, and token forcing checks every output token against stock to detect lossy changes (§3.3). Finally, validated optimizations are distilled into a structured memory as replayable code and evidence, for reuse in later rounds and new deployments.

The loop developed lossless techniques, each targeting a gap the cost model measured (§4). Best-first tree verification exploits idle drafter candidates, even on hybrid recurrent targets, and W12, a general lossless 12-bit weight format, cuts the weight reads dominating single-request steps. Two-level verification pre-checks drafts at low precision, nearly doubling accepted tokens per exact pass. For batching, three mechanisms spend verify rows where they pay off (§4.4).

We evaluate SpecPilot on four target models, three drafters, two GPU platforms and five benchmarks. Without training or quality loss, it raises the speedup over AR from stock’s 4.46×\times to 10.87×\times with one request (Figure 1), and from 1.94×\times to 3.93×\times with batching. On H100 with one request, it is 1.84×\times faster than DDTree [10].

In summary, this paper makes the following contributions:

  • [topsep=2pt,partopsep=0pt,itemsep=1pt,parsep=0pt]

  • •

    Autonomous Optimization Loop: We design SpecPilot, a ceiling-guided agentic framework that tailors speculative decoding to each deployment and transfers validated optimizations across hardware and models via a structured memory. To prevent reward hacking, we introduce token forcing, a stock-calibrated test that detects output divergences task accuracy misses.

  • •

    Discovered Lossless Algorithms: SpecPilot discovered W12, a general lossless 12-bit weight format, best-first tree verification for hybrid recurrent targets, two-level verification and three mechanisms for batching.

  • •

    Cross-Regime Bottleneck Analysis: We show how ceiling-guided discovery adapts to both memory-bandwidth and per-row compute bottlenecks, and why the same mechanism can accelerate one request but slow decoding with batching on the same GPU.

2 Background

2.1 Speculative Decoding

In speculative decoding [1, 2], a drafter proposes mm tokens x^1..m\hat{x}_{1..m} after the prefix x<tx_{<t}, and the target model verifies them in one forward pass, one row per token. Greedy decoding accepts the longest prefix with x^i=argmaxp(⋅∣x<t,x^<i)\hat{x}_{i}=\arg\max p(\cdot\mid x_{<t},\hat{x}_{<i}) and adds the target’s argmax as a bonus, accepting τ∈[1,m+1]\tau\in[1,m+1] tokens.

Lossless. A system is lossless if every accepted token lies on a path verified by a pass over the exact target weights (exact pass) and equals that pass’s argmax. Its output is then the target’s greedy decode up to floating-point reduction order, such as GEMM tiling or tree attention, which can change a token only at a logit near-tie. Stock already differs from AR in this way. At each first divergence, the two tokens’ log-probabilities differ by at most 0.232 nats (§3.3). A low-precision verify pass, by contrast, can change tokens even far from near-ties. This makes losslessness hard to test. Requiring identical outputs rejects lossless systems, and task accuracy misses faulty ones (Figure 2c). Token forcing (§3.3) instead checks every token statistically against stock.

2.2 Parallel Drafters and Draft Trees

DFlash2 [5], like DFlash [4], drafts a block of masked positions in one pass from target hidden states. A low-rank selector scores each of the top-16 candidates per position given one at the previous position, and candidates and scores form the lattice. DSpark [6] adds a Markov head on the previous token:

ℓs​(y)=bases​(y)+⟨W1​[xs−1],W2​[y]⟩,\ell_{s}(y)=\mathrm{base}_{s}(y)+\big\langle W_{1}[x_{s-1}],\,W_{2}[y]\big\rangle, (1)

where bases\mathrm{base}_{s} denotes the backbone’s logits, and stock DSpark drafts a greedy chain with it.

A draft tree contains continuations that the target verifies in one pass, each node seeing only its ancestors, and the step accepts the longest root path matching the target’s argmax plus a bonus token [7]. DDTree [10] adds nodes by path log-probability up to NN, so every prefix of this order is a best-first tree (prefix-closed).

2.3 Hybrid Targets

Our main target model, Qwen3.8-27B [14], uses Gated DeltaNet (GDN) [21] in 48 of 64 layers and attention elsewhere. A GDN head updates a fixed-size state hh per token tt by the gated delta rule,

ht=αt​(I−βt​kt​kt⊤)​ht−1+βt​kt​vt⊤,ot=ht⊤​qt,h_{t}=\alpha_{t}\big(I-\beta_{t}k_{t}k_{t}^{\top}\big)h_{t-1}+\beta_{t}k_{t}v_{t}^{\top},\qquad o_{t}=h_{t}^{\top}q_{t}, (2)

with decay gate αt\alpha_{t}, write strength βt\beta_{t}, and key, value and query kt,vt,qtk_{t},v_{t},q_{t}. Stock verification snapshots hh at each verified position, so a tree needs one snapshot per node.

3 SpecPilot

SpecPilot operates in rounds (Figure 3). A round measures where the current system loses speed (Phase 0), lets agents build and time changes (Phases 1–3) and ends with a sealed final on unseen requests (Phase 4). Each round starts from the previous round’s final system, and a new deployment from stock plus memory entries, so the loop is recursive.

3.1 Where Speculative Decoding Loses Speed

Phase 0 locates speed losses with a cost model that expresses the speedup over AR decoding as

S⁡(N)=τ⁡(N)c⁡(N),c⁡(N)=Tstep​(N)TAR,S(N)\;=\;\frac{\tau(N)}{c(N)},\qquad c(N)\;=\;\frac{T_{\mathrm{step}}(N)}{T_{\mathrm{AR}}}, (3)

where τ⁡(N)\tau(N) is the number of tokens a step accepts verifying NN rows (one per node with one request), Tstep​(N)T_{\mathrm{step}}(N) the step time with drafting and TART_{\mathrm{AR}} one AR step on the same engine. Unless otherwise stated, single-request numbers in this paper use DFlash2 and Qwen3.8-27B on an H100 GPU.

Unused candidates (τ\tau). Stock accepts far fewer tokens than its drafter’s candidates allow. In exact replay, which reruns tree selection and verification offline on recorded drafter lattices and target outputs, stock DFlash2’s 8-position chain accepts τ=4.25\tau=4.25 tokens per step (4.65 live on the bench requests of §5.1). An oracle that keeps accepting the target’s greedy token while it stays in the drafter’s top-16 would accept 6.42 at 8 positions and 8.20 at 16 (§6.4).

Weight streaming (cc, single request). With one request, reading the target’s weights dominates the step, so extra verify rows are nearly free. Before the first round, GEMM time grew only from 17.88 ms for one row to 18.58 ms for 64. After the first round, reading target weights (linears and LM head) took 80% of the measured 23.61 ms step. Even at the H100’s peak 3.35 TB/s, reading them would take 92% of the time needed to read all bytes of the step (Figure 2a).

Per-row cost (cc, batching). Each batched request adds recurrent-state and attention cost, and GEMM time steps up at each tile boundary. Each new prompt’s prefill streams the weights again. Stock DFlash2’s speedup over AR in FP8 falls from 3.40×\times with one request to 1.89×\times with 24, and on Qwen3.5-4B from 3.73×\times to 1.49×\times with 32 (Figure 2b).

Ceilings. To rank these effects, the cost model computes a ceiling for the system a round starts from. The ceiling is the speedup over that system a step could reach if it drafted once, verified the best tree in one exact pass and ran every kernel class (target GEMMs, recurrent layers, attention, drafter, prefill and the rest) at its byte floor, defined as the larger of its FLOP time at 60% of peak dense throughput and its byte time at 90% of peak bandwidth. The ceiling factors as

τbestτ⋅TprofTfloor⋅TstepTprof,\frac{\tau_{\mathrm{best}}}{\tau}\cdot\frac{T_{\mathrm{prof}}}{T_{\mathrm{floor}}}\cdot\frac{T_{\mathrm{step}}}{T_{\mathrm{prof}}}, (4)

where τ\tau and TstepT_{\mathrm{step}} are measured on the starting system, and τbest\tau_{\mathrm{best}} is the τ\tau of the best-first tree in exact replay at the best node budget. The τ\tau factor measures how many more tokens a better tree would accept. The kernel factor compares the profiled step time TprofT_{\mathrm{prof}} with the sum of its byte floors TfloorT_{\mathrm{floor}}, measuring slow kernels. The overhead factor compares TstepT_{\mathrm{step}} with TprofT_{\mathrm{prof}}, measuring time outside the profile.

Ceilings in use. Phase 0 of each round recomputes the factors from recorded lattices and profiles, and the largest factor identifies the gap. §6.1 traces them over three rounds.

3.2 Agents and Phases

SpecPilot separates the agents that modify the system from the controller that measures it (Figure 3). A master agent plans directions, one idea per GPU, each with an estimated headroom (expected gain). A sub-agent implements each direction as patches, code changes behind options whose defaults reproduce stock. A patch must pass correctness checks and token forcing (§3.3) on development requests, which agents see. The controller, scripts that agents call but cannot modify, times it against the current best in paired runs, where both systems serve the same requests on two GPUs, swapping GPUs between runs. It promotes the patch only if its gain’s 95% lower bound exceeds 1% plus twice the stock-versus-stock noise (<< 0.1% for one request on H100), or ∼{\sim}3% if its outputs diverge from the current best’s.

Phase 1: Exploration. The master starts from Phase 0’s cost model and proposes directions aimed at its largest factors. A single direction can stall on an idea that does not pay off, so the master explores the most promising few at once. A sub-agent first checks the headroom with the cheapest evidence, such as exact replay, a microbenchmark or a timing run on one GPU. It builds a new algorithm only if the headroom, net of runtime overhead, is at least 3%. It closes a direction only after measuring the implemented mechanism, unless that would take over 10 GPU-minutes.

Phases 2–3: Integration and kernel tuning. Many patches gain too little to promote alone, but enough together. An integration sub-agent stacks them on the current best and times the stack under the same rule. A kernel sub-agent profiles it and tunes kernels furthest from byte floors.

Phase 4: Sealed final. Each round ends with a sealed final, which times the system against stock on unseen requests and reruns token forcing on its outputs and on longer outputs of up to 4096 tokens. A final that fails either check is rejected.

A worked example. In round two, step cost led (§6.1), so the master opened a direction cutting weight bytes (W12, Figure 5). Byte arithmetic put its headroom at 25% of the 15.30 ms weight read, and a microbenchmark closed a denser 11-bit variant that decoded 3×\times slower. The first patch was promoted at 1.076×\times in paired runs and a revised kernel gave 1.063×\times. The DSpark, RTX PRO 6000 and Muse-Glimmer deployments reused W12 from memory (§5.3).

3.3 Token Forcing

Losslessness holds by construction (§4). Token forcing tests the implementation against stock for bugs and reward hacking. A teacher-forced scorer feeds the system’s outputs back through the target on the stock engine with an FP32 LM head. A token is a mismatch if it differs from the scorer’s argmax, and its margin is the log-probability gap to that argmax. Stock mismatches on 0.72% of tokens, almost all near-ties from kernel rounding. Phase 0 sets the near-tie threshold δ\delta by rounding up the largest margin at stock’s first departures from AR to a multiple of 1/8.

A system is rejected under either of two rules. The rate rule rejects it if its mismatch rate exceeds stock’s by more than 0.5 points at 95% confidence. The event rule rejects it if a binomial test finds its unexplained large-margin events, mismatches with margin above 2​δ2\delta, more frequent than stock’s. An audit explains an event if stock reproduces it on its own paths or margins, or if the scorer’s argmax changes with the prefill length. Figure 4 tests lossless and faulty systems.

3.4 Structured Memory

Memory lets a new deployment’s first round start from stock plus validated entries chosen by the master. After a sealed final, each promoted mechanism becomes one memory entry, holding a code delta against the entries it requires, a registry record of its variants, correctness contract and options, and a summary of its evidence, limits and untested regimes. An entry is kept only if applying it with its requirements to stock reproduces its source system’s code exactly. A reused entry is re-tuned and re-timed in the new deployment and never counts as a new discovery. The memory now holds 140 entries with up to twelve requirements each and covers every setting in §5.1 (15 entries specific to sm_120).

4 Discovered Lossless Algorithms

We describe each mechanism and why it is lossless.

4.1 W12: A Lossless 12-bit Weight Format

W12 reduces the step cost relative to AR decoding by reading fewer bytes per weight while keeping every bit exact. Most BF16 weights in an output channel span only a few binades (powers of two). For each channel nn, W12 selects the 16-binade window [En−15,En][E_{n}-15,E_{n}] that covers the most weights. Each weight with in-window exponent ee is stored as its sign bit, a 4-bit exponent offset e−(En−15)e-(E_{n}-15), and its seven mantissa bits, for a total of 12 bits (Figure 5a). Weights outside the window, zeros and denormals become escapes, which a sparse per-channel list restores exactly. W12 averages only 12.01–12.02 bits per weight on eight dense models and shrinks Qwen3.8-27B’s converted layers from 44.67 to 33.58 GB. At load time, the server checks every decoded tensor against the checkpoint bit for bit.

The GEMM kernel decodes W12 in registers, so the memory stream hides decoding. Each 12 KB record covers a 128×64128{\times}64 weight tile. It holds the 8-bit view, one byte per weight with the sign, top three mantissa bits and exponent offset (planes A and E), then the low mantissa bits (plane B). A stream-K kernel (Figure 5b) splits the reduction loop over thread blocks in a fixed order, so the GEMM is deterministic.

Certified LM head.  On H100, W12 leaves the LM head in BF16. An INT8 copy with a per-row Cauchy–Schwarz error bound discards every token that provably cannot be the argmax, and the survivors are rescored exactly. When too many survive, the full head runs instead. The argmax thus never changes. This reduces LM head latency from 878 to 482 μ\mus, outperforming W12. On the RTX PRO 6000, the certified head is slower than BF16 (2598 vs. 1750 μ\mus), so W12 converts the LM head there.

4.2 Tree Verification for Hybrid Targets

Round one built best-first trees (Figure 6) on the DFlash2 lattice, scoring each edge by log⁡softmax\log\mathrm{softmax} of selector scores given its parent, not by DDTree’s marginal scores [10]. The drafter runs 16 positions, twice its trained block size, and the tree verifies N=32N{=}32 nodes up to depth 15, more than the drafted positions (a wide tree).

Recurrent state without snapshots. SpecPilot recomputes the recurrent state along each root path instead of storing it per node. A path verify kernel walks each path from the committed state, and a commit kernel replays the accepted path into all 48 GDN layers, matching the stock kernel bit for bit on chains. The faster WY verify kernel, following TreeWY [22], turns the chain of rank-one updates in Eq. (2) into matrix products, solving all paths at once on tensor cores. It splits the FP32 state into three BF16 parts that represent all 24 significand bits exactly, accumulates tensor-core products in FP32, and stays within one BF16 ulp of the path kernel’s outputs. Both kernels change only rounding, so the exact pass stays exact.

DSpark lattice. DSpark’s Markov head scores adjacent-token pairs like the DFlash2 selector, so the best-first builder runs unchanged on a DSpark lattice that scores each child by Eq. (1) with its parent taken as xs−1x_{s-1}.

4.3 Two-Level Verification

Each TLV cycle has two passes (Figure 7). A Q pass over the 8-bit view of W12 checks the draft tree and returns the path that matches its argmax and a bonus token as a chain CC, without updating the KV cache or the recurrent state. The drafter drafts again from the end of CC, and its best-first subtree, truncated to N−|C|N-|C| nodes, is attached below CC. One exact pass over the W12 weights verifies the combined 32-node tree and accepts the longest matching path. TLV is lossless because only the exact pass accepts tokens. Under TLV, τ\tau denotes tokens per exact pass and TstepT_{\mathrm{step}} is the time of the two-pass cycle, including both drafting steps.

Zero-copy Q pass. TLV does not maintain a separate low-precision target model, since it reads the 8-bit view already nested in W12. This view is the first two thirds of each W12 record. With the dropped mantissa bits set to their midpoint, the Q pass matches the exact pass’s top-1 token at 98.7% of positions, whereas the exact pass reads the full records.

4.4 Batched Serving

Every batched row costs time (§3.1). These mechanisms only pick the rows to draft and verify, so they are lossless.

Shared node budget. Each step verifies a fixed node budget shared across requests, taking the top nodes by path log-probability. As best-first trees are prefix-closed (§2.2), each request’s share is a valid tree. On the FP8 target (Qwen3.8-27B in FP8) at 24 requests, the 192-node budget is on a plateau of the target GEMM’s cost, flat until the next tile.

Per-request drafter block. Each request drafts 16, 12 or 8 positions, chosen on the GPU from its recent acceptance and draft confidence, and its tree depth is capped to match. This keeps the FP8 target’s drafter within 256 rows, the end of the drafter GEMM’s plateau, with 17 to 24 requests.

Prompt admission. A new prompt’s rows enter the verify step, so one weight stream serves both. On the FP8 target, a prompt of up to 384 tokens enters as a chain of prompt rows, but only when the scheduler would otherwise hold it back. Both FP8 final systems admit prompts this way. For batched BF16 Qwen3.8-27B, prompts enter in 128-row segments that share the verify step’s projection and MLP GEMMs.

5 Evaluation

We examine whether the speedups hold across drafters, targets, serving regimes and GPU platforms (§5.2) and whether memory carries them to new deployments (§5.3).

5.1 Setup

Hardware and agents. Each SGLang [23] server uses one H100 SXM5 or RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition (sm_120, 1.51 TB/s measured), on a frozen v0.5.20 build, token-identical to the release. Agents are Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code [15].

Models and requests. With one request, all targets run in BF16: Qwen3.8-27B [14] with DFlash2 on both GPUs and with DSpark on H100, and Muse-Glimmer-30B [24] with DFlash2 on the RTX PRO 6000. With batching on H100, Qwen3.8-27B runs with DFlash2 or DSpark in FP8, and with DFlash2 in BF16 at 6, 8 and 10 requests as GPU memory allows. Qwen3.5-4B [25] uses DFlash2 and Gemma-4-12B [26] uses EAGLE-3, both in BF16. Requests are from GSM8K [27], HumanEval [28], MATH500 [29, 30], MBPP [31] and MT-Bench [32]. Decoding is greedy with thinking enabled, and batched clients run closed-loop with a fixed number of requests in flight (the batch size).

Metrics. A gain is the geometric mean of per-request output-rate ratios per benchmark and batch size, combined by an equal-weight geometric mean. Every gain over stock comes from a sealed final (§3.2) with two paired runs. Every final system passed token forcing. Speedups over AR (Tables 5.1 and 5.1) come from interleaved runs of AR, stock and SpecPilot on development requests, within −-2% to +6% of the sealed gains on unseen requests.
